about: Bringing an object into being, at an id the client picked. The verb v0 did not have — added because the first application to live entirely on this format could read a library, follow it, and patch it, and had to reach past the binding to make a single note.

cases.why: The base case, and the one the format could not say at all until now. A client that can read a library and change what is in it and cannot add to it is not usable as an application; it is a viewer with edit buttons.

Identity says an id is opaque and does not say who mints it, which always permitted this and never provided the verb. The client choosing is not a convenience: it is the whole mechanism behind the next two cases, because an id decided before the request is what makes a repeat recognizable as a repeat.

A queue that drained on a bad network sent this twice and heard the answer once. It must not produce two radiators. `created: false` is how a client learns its retry was not the one that landed — success either way, and the distinction available to whoever wants it.

The reason this verb creates and never edits. A PUT that replaced would be the round-trip rule broken at write time by the verb least likely to be suspected of it: the client sends the fields it knows about, and status and owner — which it has never heard of — are gone. Changing an object is PATCH's job, where absent already means absent.
A body id that disagrees with the address is a client bug, and picking one is how an object is created somewhere nobody will look for it. Refusing is the only answer that cannot be silently wrong.

A producer may accept this and may refuse it. What it must not do is accept it, invent a type, and answer a bare ok — which is loud failure applied to the one write that has no prior object to compare against.

The round-trip rule holds at the moment of creation too. A producer that keeps only the properties its types declare turns every create into a lossy import, and the loss is invisible because there is no earlier version to compare with.
